method: The key is read as a letter A to G with up to two sharps or flats, giving the tonic pitch. In the chords to numbers direction each chord token is a root, a quality suffix and an optional slash bass; the root may carry up to two sharps or flats and the suffix is scanned from a fixed vocabulary (m, M, maj, min, dim, aug, sus, add, alt, no, degree and half-diminished signs, digits, altered digits such as b9 or #11, and brackets). The degree number is the semitone distance from the tonic taken on the major scale: 0 semitones is 1, 2 is 2, 4 is 3, 5 is 4, 7 is 5, 9 is 6 and 11 is 7; the five remaining distances are written with a flat as b2, b3, b5, b6 and b7, so F sharp in C becomes b5 rather than #4. The quality suffix and the bar lines are copied through unchanged, so G7 in C is 57 and Am7 is 6m7, and a slash bass note is numbered the same way, so C/E is 1/3 and C/Bb is 1/b7. In the numbers to chords direction a token is an optional b or # (at most two), a degree 1 to 7, the same quality vocabulary and an optional slash degree. The chord root keeps the letter of that degree of the key, so the seventh degree of C sharp is B sharp and the seventh of C flat is B flat, and the accidental is the difference between the degree's pitch and that letter's natural pitch, which is why b3 in C is E flat and #4 in D is G sharp. Bars are the non-empty groups between bar lines. A key is refused when its major scale needs more than two accidentals on any degree, which rules out theoretical spellings such as F double flat. A chart holds at most 200 chords; six-nine chords are refused because a slash always means a bass note, and mixed sharps and flats, unknown qualities, a missing bass and a degree outside 1 to 7 are refused with the offending token named. Numbers are measured from the major scale, so a minor-key song uses its relative major: Am-F-C-G in C is 6m 4 1 5. The page does not model key signatures, roman numerals, superscription, repeat signs, pushes or chord voicings, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Nashville Number System: numbers denote the scale degree a chord is built on, accidentals are written to the left of the number, minor chords use a dash or lowercase m, and a slash gives the bass note's scale degree (1/3 is the 1 chord with the third in the bass).
Hudson Valley Bluegrass Association, The Nashville Number System: in C the numbers run C Dm Em F G7 Am B(m7b5), so chord quality follows the major scale and the number chart works in any key.
Jack W. Cannon, Introduction to the Nashville Numbering System: only b and # may be prepended to a degree number, and chord-type modifiers follow it.
